1.) We recommend installing a wet switch by the condensate pump in the attic. This will prevent the system from running and dumping water into the attic space should the condensate pump and internal safety switch fail for any reason. 

2.) The systems can both use an in-depth cleaning. This helps to keep the systems running properly and efficiently. Photos of the cleanliness of the systems (particular emphasis on the blowers) will be included on the system evaluation form. 

3.) We also recommend installing a more premium air filter for both units. This will decrease restrictions to airflow while also providing better filtration. Additionally, the one inch filters currently used should be changed every 30 days. The new AprilAire media filters can last 6-12 months between changes.

i.313600655:
Today, I completed the annual electrical system inspection. During my evaluation, I found that most of the baseboard outlets are ungrounded. Ungrounded receptacles are a safety concern, particularly when three-prong appliances or equipment are plugged into them. In the event of an electrical fault, an improperly grounded system can create a potential shock hazard by allowing energized metal components to become electrically charged.

I also observed that the main electrical panel is advanced in age. Due to the age of the equipment, replacement is recommended. Electrical panels and their internal safety components can deteriorate over time, and older circuit breakers may become less reliable and may fail to trip properly during an overload or fault condition. This can increase the risk of overheating and electrical damage.

Additionally, the building’s water piping system is not properly bonded/grounded. A properly sized grounding/bonding conductor should be installed from the main electrical service to the water piping system near the water meter. This provides a proper path for fault current and helps reduce the risk of electrical shock when using metal plumbing fixtures.

The customer advised that they will address the ungrounded receptacles. However, they requested an estimate for replacement of the main electrical panel and installation of the required water-piping grounding/bonding connection.

All available solutions were presented to the customer. An estimate for the requested work was provided separately.

Today, I completed the annual electrical system inspection. During my evaluation, I found the main electrical panel to be zinsco panel. Zinsco panels were recalled in the early 1980s due to known fire hazards associated with the breakers failing to trip properly. When breakers do not trip as designed, excessive heat can build up in the breakers, wiring, and connected equipment, creating a potential fire hazard.

Due to the age and safety concerns associated with this panel, replacement of the main electrical panel is strongly recommended. These panels are considered unsafe, and replacement breakers and components may no longer be readily available if an existing breaker fails.

I also found several three-prong receptacles that are not properly grounded. Ungrounded three-prong outlets do not provide the intended equipment-grounding protection and can present a safety hazard. In the event of an electrical fault, exposed metal components or equipment could potentially become energized. The homeowner said he will adress the outlets.

I recommend replacing the existing two-prong and ungrounded receptacles with properly installed GFCI-protected receptacles, as applicable, to improve safety and bring the electrical system into compliance with current requirements where permitted.

The wiring connection points and lugs have developed oxidation from moisture exposure, potentially compromising the integrity of the electrical connections. The upstairs panel disconnect also contains a discontinued Zinsco breaker, which is associated with known safety concerns, including potential failure to trip during an overcurrent condition and an increased risk of overheating and electrical fires. Additionally, deterioration was observed affecting the electronic driver components of the existing arc-fault circuit interrupter (AFCI) breaker in the upstairs electrical panel.

LPH also identified an opportunity to improve the home’s protection against transient voltage spikes through the installation of a whole-home surge protector. The exterior receptacles were found to lack GFCI protection, and several devices were deteriorated or equipped with improper covers. Recommendations include replacing the affected exterior receptacles with weather-resistant devices, installing GFCI protection where needed, and adding properly rated in-use bubble covers to help protect against moisture intrusion.

The findings and recommended improvements were discussed thoroughly with the homeowner who was present at the time of the visit. e.344271519:
LPH arrived at the residence to evaluate the existing electrical system and discuss recommended improvements to enhance electrical safety, reliability, and protection throughout the home.

Basement Trough and Disconnect Replacement:

Upon inspection, LPH identified extensive rust and corrosion within the existing basement electrical trough, indicating a history of water intrusion and moisture exposure. The moisture has affected the wiring connections, leaving a film of oxidation and corrosion on the connection points and lugs. Corroded connections can increase electrical resistance, generate excessive heat, and compromise the reliability of the electrical system.

Additionally, the disconnect supplying the upstairs bedroom electrical panel has exceeded its recommended service life and shows considerable rust and corrosion throughout the enclosure. The internal lugs have also developed oxidation and corrosion, further compromising the integrity of the electrical connections. This disconnect contains a discontinued Zinsco breaker, a product line widely associated with serious safety concerns, including breakers that may fail to trip during an overload or short circuit, overheating, and connections that can deteriorate over time. These concerns can increase the risk of electrical fires and may also create complications during insurance reviews or real estate transactions.

LPH recommends replacing the existing trough and disconnect arrangement with a new electrical trough mounted securely to a backer board. The existing wiring will be reconnected using heavy-duty Polaris insulated connectors, providing secure, reliable connections. A new 100-amp disconnect will also be installed on the backer board to supply the upstairs electrical panel. This replacement will eliminate the deteriorated equipment and outdated disconnect, improve the integrity of the electrical connections, and provide a safer, more dependable electrical distribution setup.

Whole-Home Surge Protection:

During the inspection, LPH also identified deterioration affecting the electronic driver components of the arc-fault circuit interrupter (AFCI) breaker in the upstairs electrical panel. This is the only AFCI breaker currently installed in the home. Electronic components can experience wear and deterioration over time from transient voltage spikes that occur throughout a home’s electrical system. These voltage fluctuations can be generated when motor-driven equipment, such as air conditioners, refrigerators, and other appliances, cycles on and off. Utility-related disturbances and lightning can also introduce damaging voltage surges.

LPH recommends installing a premium whole-home surge protector at the electrical service equipment. This device helps limit damaging transient overvoltages before they reach connected circuits and sensitive electronic equipment. By reducing exposure to these voltage spikes, whole-home surge protection can help protect appliance control boards, televisions, computers, and other valuable electronics, potentially extending their service life and reducing the likelihood of costly premature failures. While no surge protector can eliminate every electrical threat, this upgrade provides an additional layer of protection for the home’s electrical system and connected equipment.

Exterior Receptacle Safety Improvements:

During the evaluation, LPH discovered that the exterior receptacles lack GFCI protection and that two of the existing receptacles have improper covers. The receptacles currently installed are intended for indoor use and have deteriorated significantly from prolonged exposure to outdoor conditions. Moisture intrusion and corrosion can compromise receptacle connections, increase the likelihood of electrical failures, and create potential shock hazards.

LPH recommends replacing the affected exterior receptacles with weather-resistant devices designed for outdoor applications. The proposed improvements include one weather-resistant receptacle, three weather-resistant GFCI receptacles, and two extra-duty in-use bubble covers. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of serious electrical shock by quickly interrupting power when a ground fault is detected. The weather-resistant receptacles and properly rated covers will provide improved protection against rain, moisture, and environmental exposure. The in-use bubble covers are designed to help protect receptacles while cords are plugged in, providing an additional layer of protection against water intrusion.

These improvements will address the deteriorated exterior devices, bring the receptacle installations closer to current safety expectations, and provide more dependable outdoor electrical service.

LPH recommends completing these improvements to address the existing corrosion, eliminate the outdated Zinsco disconnect, improve electrical connection reliability, and add protection against electrical shock and damaging voltage surges. Together, these upgrades will help improve the overall safety, reliability, and long-term performance of the home’s electrical system.

i.331406411:
This afternoon I arrived at the Ternoski family home to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon my arrival, Mr. Ternoski informed me that they had accidentally overloaded the circuit which they are using to supply power to their RV. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the circuit I do un there to be no tripped breakers, and all breaker were providing 120v of power (at minimum), yet no power was reaching the garage. I began to conduct a very thorough analysis of all devices, both known and unknown, that could potentially be on this circuit. I found no discrepancies. From there I entered the homes crawl space which spans the homes entire footprint minus the garage. I located the entry from most of the homes circuits to the breaker panel and found several discrepancies. I found improper and unsafe Junctioning means, including open junctions and splices, improperly located and unweatherized “in-wall” splices free hanging. More concerning yet, I noted that the homes dryer vent is vented almost directly onto these improper junctions. What this has done is created a thick film of dryer lint on these already potentially hazardous junctions. I have included photos of my findings, and provided an option to essentially dismantle, and properly reinstall all of these non code-compliant splices. 

Circling back to the loss of power, after digging through several of the junctions, I identified one bundle of wires which had too many hot wires under one wire nut. It appeared that one wire had been worked loose of the wire nut, and potentially further loosened during our overload event. I retracted this circuit and worked out which wires were live from the bundle in order to separate the cluster of wires properly using appropriately sized wire nuts. I was able to restore power to the garage, and also identified that the garage was being powered by a breaker labeled as “master bedroom”.

Finally I provided an estimate to run an appropriate dedicated 30A circuit and plug for the RV, as to avoid potential overloads down the road. 

If you have any questions, concerns, or if you would like to move forward with any of today’s provided estimates, please do not hesitate to reach out. Thank you for your patience today, and I look forward to our next visit!

All other electrical components throughout the home were tested and were found to be functioning properly.

However, I did identify an issue with the home’s grounding and bonding system. The grounding system consists of two primary components: the grounding electrode system (ground rods) and the bonding of the home’s metal water and gas piping.

The required bonding connection from the main electrical panel to the water piping is currently missing. A properly sized copper bonding conductor should be installed from the main electrical panel to the appropriate locations on the water piping, including the house and street sides of the water meter, with the gas piping properly bonded as required.

Proper bonding helps ensure that metal piping, gas appliances, water fixtures, and other conductive components throughout the home remain at the same electrical potential and provides a safe path for fault current back to the electrical system.

As the system currently stands, there is a potential shock hazard in the event of an electrical fault involving the gas piping, water piping, appliances, or other metal components.

Recommended Solution

Provide and install the required bonding connections to properly bond the home’s water and gas piping to the electrical grounding system and bring the system into proper compliance.

A water softener is a system that removes the minerals responsible for hard water, primarily calcium and magnesium. If you're considering a soft water system for your city water supply, it can make a noticeable difference in your plumbing, appliances, cleaning routine, and bathing experience.
One important distinction: city water and soft water are not the same thing. City water is treated by your municipal water utility to meet drinking-water standards, but it can still contain substantial amounts of calcium and magnesium. A home water softener reduces those minerals before the water flows through your house.
The major benefits of a water softener
1. Less scale buildup on faucets, showers, and fixtures
Hard water leaves chalky white deposits on showerheads, faucets, glass shower doors, and sinks. Soft water dramatically reduces these mineral deposits, so your bathroom and kitchen stay cleaner and require less scrubbing.
2. Longer life for household appliances
Mineral scale can accumulate inside water heaters, dishwashers, washing machines, and other water-using appliances. Softening can reduce that buildup, help maintain efficiency, and potentially extend equipment life, particularly in areas with very hard water.
3. Softer-feeling skin after showering
Hard water can leave mineral residue on your skin. Soft water reduces that residue and may help some people feel less dry or tight after bathing. It does not treat skin conditions, and results vary by person.
4. Hair that feels easier to manage
With fewer mineral deposits left on your hair, you may notice less residue, improved softness, and easier combing. The effect depends on your hair type, products, and the hardness of your original water.
5. Cleaner dishes and glassware
Soft water helps prevent cloudy spots and white mineral film on glasses, plates, and silverware. You may also be able to reduce dishwasher detergent and rinse-aid use, following your appliance manufacturer's instructions.
6. Softer laundry and towels
Hard-water minerals can interfere with detergents and leave residue in fabrics. Soft water can help towels feel softer, clothes look brighter, and laundry rinse more effectively.
7. More lather from soap and shampoo
Calcium and magnesium react with soap and reduce its effectiveness. Soft water allows soap, shampoo, and body wash to lather more easily, so you may need less product to get the same result.
8. Better water-heater performance
Hard-water scale can build up on heating elements and inside tanks. Reducing scale may improve heat transfer and help prevent maintenance problems. The amount of energy saved depends on how hard your water is and the condition and type of your water heater.
9. Less time spent cleaning
You will generally spend less time removing hard-water rings, soap scum, and mineral crust from bathroom fixtures, shower doors, sinks, and tubs. Existing heavy deposits may still need to be cleaned off first.
10. Less soap scum in bathrooms
Soft water reduces the formation of insoluble soap deposits caused by hard-water minerals. This can mean less sticky film on tubs, shower walls, and shower curtains.
11. Reduced mineral buildup in plumbing
A properly sized and maintained softener can reduce scale inside pipes, valves, and plumbing fixtures. This is especially useful where hard water would otherwise cause substantial buildup over time. It does not repair existing corrosion or remove every type of plumbing deposit.
12. Potential savings on household products
Because soft water makes cleaning products and soaps work more effectively, you may spend less on laundry detergent, dishwashing products, shampoo, and soap. Your savings depend on your current water hardness, product use, and the cost of maintaining the softener.

I found a loose receptacle in the bathroom, likely due to age and frequent use. A loose outlet can create an unsafe connection and should be secured or replaced as necessary. I presented the homeowner with the option to replace the existing duplex receptacle.

Found several other concerns during visit today. In the utility room, identified the laundry faucet is leaking down through sink on concrete floor. Kitchen faucet upstairs is loose and in poor condition. Also in the upstairs bathroom, the tub spout is faulty and not diverting the water properly.

Went over all suggestions and recommendations based on the plumbing inspection today. Homeowner approved the drain rebuild and drain cleaning service today. i.339059985:
Out to home today for the yearly plumbing system check. Upon arrival to home, there were two concerns in regards to the plumbing. 

First concern has to do with requesting pricing on installation of a new drinking water system. They currently have one installed, however the unit is disconnected and not functioning. They would like a new one installed and then have a line connected to the existing faucet and over to the fridge. 
Second concern has to do with the powder room sink. They had jewelry fall down the drain. They took apart the drain and was able to retrieve the lost item. They are requesting for the sink to be reconnected under neath. Upon evaluation, found that the pop-up drain is old and corroded and should be replaced as well. Provided solution of replacing pop-up drain and reconnecting sink. 

From there, performed the full home plumbing inspection today. During inspection, performed routine flush of water heater system. Performed water quality test and verified function of softener system. Also tested water pressure to be within a safe threshold inside the home at about 60 PSI. 

Found several concerns during the inspection today. 

At the kitchen sink, found that the garbage disposal is not working and over 10 years old. The kitchen faucet leaks from the base and down into the cabinet below. The old drainage is corroded and there is an open hole in the drop where the old RO drained into. In the powder room, found a leak coming from the tank of the toilet. In the full bathroom at the front of the home, the toilet is out of commission due to a previous leak. They stated that the toilet had been shut off for about 3 years. LPH will need to perform major rebuild of toilet tank and reset seal from base of fixture. Recommended replacement of fixture due to condition. In both upstairs bathrooms, the tub spout leaks quite a bit when running the shower reducing quantity and volume of hot water during showers. 

In the Basement, found that the water softener unit is extremely aged being installed back in 2001. Suggested replacement of unit due to being over the expected lifespan for the system. Found whole home expansion tank to have failed and is not able to react and absorb changes to water pressure. This will cause pressure spikes inside the home and lead to failure of plumbing components. At the water heater system, the condensation drains onto the floor then into a ground water pit. Suggested rerouting condensate into pump system to discharge into the sewer. Lastly, the outdoor faucets on the back and front of the home leaks when in use. 

Went over all recommendations and pricing for repairs. Pricing provided today is valid for 60 days. 

If you found value in the inspection today, LPH highly recommends signing up for our membership program to have these inspections performed every year. Left information behind about plan. If there are any questions about the quotes that were provided today, please do not hesitate to reach out to our office. Thank you for trusting LPH.

Upon evaluating the dryer, I found that the dryer itself appears to have an internal failure or a failed component, which is causing it not to operate properly. The issue does not appear to be related to the home’s electrical supply.

Due to their age, there is an increased likelihood of breaker and other component failures, which can contribute to electrical distribution problems and potential safety concerns. The panels are Sylvania panels, which are known to have issues with breakers failing to trip properly under certain fault conditions. A breaker that fails to trip when required can allow excessive current to continue flowing, potentially resulting in overheating or damage to connected electrical components.

Based on the age, condition, accessibility, and manufacturer of the existing equipment, I informed homeowner both 200-amp main electrical panels need to be replaced to improve electrical safety, reliability, and proper power distribution throughout the home.

I also explained that the existing cabinet will need to be modified or removed as necessary to provide proper access when the panels are replaced. In addition, surge protection will need to be installed at the main panels as part of the panel replacement to meet current code requirements. Themis didn’t want anything els checked during today visit.

LPH performed a comprehensive electrical system check to evaluate the condition, safety, and reliability of the home’s electrical components. During the inspection, the homeowner’s concerns regarding nonfunctioning electrical devices led to further investigation, revealing extensive deterioration and potentially dangerous conditions throughout the home.

Switches and Receptacles: Upon opening device boxes and examining the existing wiring connections, LPH discovered widespread damage associated with the existing backstab wiring method. Nearly every device inspected showed significant deterioration, including heat-related cracking, broken device housings, loose conductors, and electrical arcing. In some instances, minimal movement while inspecting the devices caused components to break apart, wires to short together, and arcing to occur. During today’s system check, LPH identified 22 single-pole switches, 7 three-way switches, 5 duplex receptacles, and 1 dimmer switch exhibiting serious damage or unsafe connections. Due to the extent of the deterioration, LPH recommends replacing all switches and duplex receptacles throughout the home rather than limiting repairs to devices that have already failed. Devices that appear intact externally may still have compromised internal connections, and additional devices may be affected because not every device box could be opened and inspected within the available timeframe.

Kitchen GFCI Protection: LPH identified a failed GFCI receptacle protecting the kitchen countertop circuit. The device is no longer tripping as intended, leaving the portion of the circuit it protects without functioning ground-fault protection. Replacement is recommended to restore this important protection against electrical shock.

Exterior Meter Base and Service Cable: LPH also evaluated concerns regarding possible water intrusion at the exterior meter base. Small amounts of water intrusion were suspected within the meter base enclosure. Visible rust was present along one side of the electrical panel, and corrosion was observed on the service cable near its outer jacket. These findings raise concerns regarding continued moisture exposure and potential deterioration of the electrical service components. LPH recommends inspecting and resealing the exterior meter base entry points with appropriate exterior-rated sealant and replacing the existing service cable between the meter base and interior electrical panel. The accessible service equipment and cable entry points should also be inspected for additional moisture-related damage, with the electrical service tested upon completion of the repairs.

Immediate Safety Repairs: Due to the severity of the damaged electrical connections identified during the inspection, one three-way switch was approved by the homeowner for immediate replacement today because leaving the damaged device connected presented an imminent electrical safety concern. The remaining recommendations address additional hazards and proactive improvements intended to reduce the risk of overheating, electrical arcing, electrical shock, and potential fire.

Estimates and Follow-Up: LPH reviewed the findings and recommendations identified during today’s system check. The homeowner approved the immediate replacement of the damaged three-way switch. The remaining estimates, including the comprehensive whole-home switch and receptacle replacement and the exterior meter base sealing and service cable replacement, will be emailed to the trust for review and consideration. Today’s electrical evaluation and supporting photographs documenting the observed conditions will also be provided for review.

LPH will follow up with a phone call on Monday to discuss the estimates, answer any questions, and determine how the trust would like to proceed with the remaining recommended work.

Thank you for allowing LPH to evaluate the home’s electrical system. We appreciate the opportunity to identify these concerns and provide recommendations to help improve the home’s electrical safety and reliability.

A Moen Flo is a smart water leak detection and automatic shutoff system that helps protect your home from costly water damage. Think of it as a security system for your home's plumbing: it monitors your water 24/7 and can automatically turn off the main water supply when it detects a potential serious leak.

1. Helps prevent expensive water damage
If a pipe bursts, a supply line breaks, or water runs abnormally, Flo can detect the problem and shut off the main water supply to limit flooding. This can be particularly valuable when you're sleeping or away on vacation.
2. Detects hidden leaks
Its daily MicroLeak tests can identify leaks as small as approximately one drop per minute. That may help you catch a slow leak behind a wall or from a plumbing fixture before it causes major damage. ￼
3. Sends alerts to your phone
You can receive notifications about unusual water usage and possible leaks, helping you respond quickly whether you're at home, at work, or traveling.
4. Lets you monitor water usage
See water consumption, flow rate, pressure, and usage history. This can help identify a running toilet, an unnoticed leak, or other unnecessary water consumption.
5. Provides peace of mind while traveling
You can check your home's water system remotely and turn the water off through the app. Automatic shutoff can be especially useful if a leak occurs while no one is home.
6. May help with insurance costs
Some insurance companies offer discounts for qualifying leak-prevention systems. Eligibility and savings depend on your insurer and policy, so check before purchasing.

i.339797874:
Completed cooling system check on two Trane units, a Goodman, and performed a heating system check on a Dornback gas furnace. At this time 2 out of the 4 units are operating properly and within spec. Measurements for all can be referred to on their system evaluation forms. 

Spend a decent amount of time this visit trying to find the source of an intermittent shut off for the Dornback. Everything I checked (which was an extensive diagnosis) seemed to be operating properly. No obstruction was found in any of the air passages, blower was operating properly, and burner assembly was properly set up. All that being said, combustion was still very short of perfect (refer to evaluation form). CO2 was very high and O2 was very low. The unit was burning very hot (around 550 F), but CO was zero. There seems to be serious efficiency issues with the unit and no one particular issue present. Given age of the unit, I spoke to Lemma about the possibility of replacing the unit for something more efficient and appropriately sized for the space (current is much too large). They would like to hold off talking about replacement, but if issues occur over the winter they’ll reach out. 

The Trane unit for the basement cooling needs was critically low on charge. I was told that the unit was charge about 3 years ago, so there is more than likely a leak present somewhere in the system. Given age of system (30 yrs), it would be ill-advised to perform any sort of repair on the system, if even possible. They would still like to hold off on any replacement talk at this time.

i.340066220:
LPH arrived at the home to perform a comprehensive electrical system check and discuss the homeowners’ future plans for the property. During the evaluation, we reviewed the existing electrical system, discussed current concerns, and explored several improvements to help accommodate the homeowners’ planned basement renovations and future electrical needs.

Basement Electrical Rewiring and Future Improvements

We discussed the existing basement electrical layout, which currently relies heavily on a single circuit supplying the basement lighting and receptacles, exterior receptacles, screened-in porch receptacles, and kitchen island receptacle. With the planned basement improvements, including a kitchenette, exercise area, fireplace heater, radon fan, and inflatable hot tub, adding dedicated circuits and redistributing the existing electrical loads will provide a more functional electrical layout and help reduce the likelihood of nuisance tripping.

LPH provided an estimate to rewire the unfinished basement with six new circuits, including dedicated circuits for the radon fan, exercise equipment, kitchenette, fireplace heater, exterior hot tub, and general basement receptacles. The proposed work also includes transferring the upstairs kitchen island receptacle to the new kitchenette circuit, installing the appropriate AFCI/GFCI protection, and transitioning the existing wiring through accessible junction boxes to maintain continuity for the remaining circuits.

We also discussed adding a new 20-amp circuit from the main electrical panel to provide receptacles inside the garage and outside the home. This will provide a more appropriate power source for the garage microwave and eliminate the need to rely on an extension cord plugged into the garage door opener receptacle.

Exterior Receptacle Repairs and Whole-Home Surge Protection

During our discussion, we reviewed the condition of the existing exterior receptacles and the importance of maintaining proper weather protection and GFCI protection in outdoor locations. LPH provided an estimate to replace the damaged receptacles with new weather-resistant devices, including two weather-resistant GFCI receptacles and two weather-resistant duplex receptacles, utilizing the existing appropriate bubble covers.

We also discussed installing whole-home surge protection to help protect sensitive electronics, appliances, and other electrical equipment from damaging voltage surges originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, and electrical equipment cycling within the home. This additional protection is particularly beneficial when investing in new electrical equipment and modern circuit protection.

Grounding and Bonding Improvements

We discussed the existing grounding and bonding system, which requires additional attention to address the incomplete grounding arrangement. LPH provided an additional estimate to install an appropriate grounding clamp and connection at the existing metal water line, where applicable, and add approximately five feet of grounding conductor to bond the home’s gas piping system as required by applicable electrical code.

Proper grounding and bonding help establish an intentional path for electrical fault current and reduce potentially dangerous voltage differences between metal piping systems and other grounded components throughout the home.

Main Electrical Panel Replacement

We also discussed the existing 200-amp Crouse-Hinds electrical panel, which is approximately 34 years old. Although the panel is rated for 200 amps, its age warrants consideration of replacement as the homeowners continue making improvements to the property and adding electrical loads.

LPH provided a separate estimate to replace the existing panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH panel. This upgrade will provide modern electrical distribution equipment, additional circuit spaces for future projects, and an opportunity to evaluate the existing service connections, breaker connections, grounding, bonding, and neutral terminations.

Replacing the panel proactively will help improve long-term serviceability and provide a better foundation for the home’s future electrical needs. We also discussed incorporating whole-home surge protection as part of the overall electrical improvement plan.

Review of Options and Plans Moving Forward

All recommendations and available options were discussed with the homeowner in relation to the property’s current electrical conditions and the planned basement improvements. Separate estimates have been prepared to allow the homeowners to review the proposed work, compare the options, and determine how they would like to proceed.

We will carve out time tomorrow morning to fully discuss the estimates, answer any remaining questions, prioritize the recommended improvements, and determine the best plan moving forward.

Today’s electrical system check evaluation and all associated estimates will be emailed to the homeowners for their review.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to evaluate your electrical system and discuss your future plans for the property. We look forward to speaking with you tomorrow morning and servicing you again in the future.

e.345072708:
LPH will rewire the unfinished basement and install six new dedicated circuits from the existing basement subpanel. This upgrade will provide properly distributed electrical service for the basement’s current and planned uses, reduce the electrical load on the existing circuits, and provide the appropriate protection for the new receptacles and connected equipment.

Basement Rewiring – Six New Circuits

1. Dedicated 15-Amp Radon Fan Circuit

* Install one new 15-amp circuit dedicated to the radon fan.
* Install a single receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall to provide a protected wiring method.

This dedicated circuit will provide a separate power source for the radon fan rather than relying on a shared circuit serving other basement equipment and receptacles.

2. Dedicated 20-Amp Exercise Area Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the basement exercise area.
* Install three receptacles to accommodate the designated exercise equipment.
* Install two receptacles along the wall bordering the mechanical room.
* Reuse the existing conduit at the designated location, remove the existing receptacle wiring, and install new wiring and a new receptacle.

Providing a dedicated circuit for the exercise area will help accommodate the electrical demand of the equipment without adding additional loads to the general basement receptacle circuit.

3. Dedicated 20-Amp Basement Kitchenette Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the planned basement kitchenette.
* Install two receptacle locations at the designated areas.
* Pick up the upstairs kitchen island receptacle as part of this circuit using wiring accessible from the basement.

Including the upstairs kitchen island receptacle on this new circuit will help remove its load from the existing circuit serving the basement lighting, screened-in porch, and existing exterior receptacles. This will help distribute the electrical demand more appropriately and reduce the likelihood of nuisance tripping on the existing circuit.

This circuit will provide a separate power source for the kitchenette and kitchen island receptacles, helping distribute the electrical load as the basement living space is developed.

4. Dedicated 20-Amp Fireplace Heater Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit dedicated to the basement fireplace heater.
* Install one receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall.

A dedicated circuit will help accommodate the heater’s electrical demand without unnecessarily loading the general-purpose basement receptacle circuit.

5. Dedicated 20-Amp Exterior Hot Tub Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit from the basement subpanel, routed across the basement and drilled through the exterior wall to the back porch.
* Install one weather-resistant GFCI receptacle with an appropriate in-use bubble cover to supply the 120-volt inflatable hot tub.

Because this receptacle will serve equipment used around water, proper ground-fault protection is particularly important. GFCI protection is designed to quickly interrupt power when an electrical fault creates a potentially dangerous shock hazard.

The final circuit and receptacle arrangement will need to meet the hot tub manufacturer’s electrical requirements and applicable code requirements for the installation location.

6. Dedicated 20-Amp General Basement Receptacle Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the remaining designated basement receptacles.
* Reuse the existing conduit at one location and install a new receptacle.
* Cut in one receptacle along the stairway wall.
* Install three additional receptacles at the designated locations, using conduit down the block walls as needed.

This additional circuit will provide convenient receptacle access throughout the basement while distributing the electrical demand across multiple circuits instead of continuing to rely on the existing overloaded arrangement.

Basement Circuit Protection

The six new circuits will be installed from the existing basement subpanel using the appropriate wiring methods and circuit protection for their intended applications. The estimate includes:

* Four 20-amp dual-function AFCI/GFCI circuit breakers.
* One 20-amp AFCI circuit breaker.
* One 15-amp AFCI circuit breaker.

AFCI protection is designed to detect certain dangerous electrical arcing conditions that can lead to fires. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock by detecting ground faults and interrupting power. Dual-function breakers combine both protective features in one device.

The specified breakers will provide the intended protection for the new circuits while helping bring the installation into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements.

Existing Basement Wiring – Junction Box Transition

Currently, one existing circuit supplies the basement lighting and receptacles, exterior receptacles, screened-in porch receptacles, and kitchen island receptacle. This places a substantial number of electrical loads on a single circuit and can contribute to nuisance tripping when multiple devices are operating.

As part of this project, LPH will disconnect and transition the existing basement wiring as necessary, installing accessible junction boxes along the basement ceiling to maintain continuity for the existing circuits. This will allow the existing wiring to remain operational while the new circuits take over the designated basement receptacle loads and the upstairs kitchen island receptacle is transferred to the new kitchenette circuit.

The goal is to distribute the electrical demand more appropriately, reduce the burden on the existing circuit, and provide a more functional electrical layout for the basement and the home’s connected areas.

Whole-Home Surge Protection Recommendation

With the installation of multiple new circuits and sensitive AFCI/GFCI protective devices, LPH recommends adding a whole-home surge protector at the main electrical panel.

Modern electrical equipment, appliances, and electronic circuit boards can be damaged by voltage surges originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, or electrical equipment cycling on and off within the home. These events can also contribute to premature wear or damage to sensitive electronic components.

A whole-home surge protector provides an additional layer of defense by helping divert damaging transient voltage away from the home’s electrical system and connected equipment. It is particularly beneficial for homes with modern appliances, HVAC equipment, electronics, and other sensitive devices.

Although surge protection cannot prevent every type of electrical disturbance or guarantee that equipment will never be damaged, it is a worthwhile protective upgrade for the home.

Additional 20-Amp Exterior Circuit From the Main Panel

LPH will install one additional 20-amp circuit from the main electrical panel to supply two receptacles serving the main garage area: one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel and one exterior receptacle on the opposite side of the wall.

This installation will include:

* Routing the new circuit from the main panel and dropping down the wall to the designated locations.
* Installing a GFCI-protected receptacle at the designated exterior location.
* Installing one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel.
* Providing convenient power sources for both interior garage and exterior use.
* Providing a more suitable power source for the garage microwave, reducing reliance on the existing garage door opener receptacle and extension cord.

Currently, the microwave is being powered through the garage door opener receptacle using an extension cord. This is not an ideal arrangement for an appliance that draws substantial current, particularly when the circuit may already be supplying other equipment. A properly installed receptacle on a new circuit will provide a more appropriate power source and help reduce nuisance tripping caused by shared electrical loads.

Exterior Receptacle Repairs and Weather Protection

LPH will also address the damaged exterior receptacles by replacing the existing devices with new weather-resistant receptacles and providing the required GFCI protection.

This portion of the work includes:

* Two weather-resistant GFCI receptacles.
* Two weather-resistant duplex receptacles.
* Reuse of the existing boxes and appropriate bubble covers where suitable.

Weather-resistant receptacles are designed to better withstand outdoor environmental exposure. Combined with appropriate GFCI protection and suitable covers, these replacements will help reduce the risk of moisture-related deterioration, electrical faults, and shock hazards.

The existing boxes are already equipped with appropriate bubble covers, so the existing covers will be retained where they are in suitable condition and compatible with the new receptacles.

Additional Grounding and Bonding Improvements

LPH recommends completing the home’s grounding and bonding system by installing a grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and adding approximately 5 feet of grounding conductor to bond the home’s gas piping system as required by applicable electrical code.

e.345090633:
LPH recommends replacing the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel with a brand-new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while retaining the home’s existing 200-amp service capacity.

Although the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is rated for 200 amps, its age and original design make replacement a worthwhile investment in the home’s electrical safety, reliability, and ability to accommodate modern electrical demands. Electrical panels are responsible for distributing power throughout the home and providing overcurrent protection to individual circuits. As panels age, breakers and internal connection points can experience wear, deterioration, and reduced reliability. Breaker connections on the bus bar can also loosen over time, potentially causing overheating, arcing, or unreliable circuit operation.

Why Upgrade the Existing Panel?

1. Aging Electrical Equipment

At approximately 34 years old, the existing Crouse-Hinds panel has provided decades of service. However, its age warrants consideration of replacement before deterioration or component failures create a more urgent situation. Replacing the panel allows LPH to install new equipment rather than continuing to depend on aging internal components and connections.

2. Better Support for Today’s Electrical Demands

Modern homes typically place greater demands on their electrical systems than they did decades ago. Today’s households rely on larger appliances, home office equipment, entertainment systems, exercise equipment, electronic devices, and other electrical loads that may not have been anticipated when the original panel was installed.

The existing panel’s 200-amp rating does not automatically mean the home needs a larger service. However, replacing the older panel provides an opportunity to improve circuit organization, evaluate the home’s electrical distribution, and accommodate additional circuit protection and future electrical projects where capacity permits.

3. Upgrade to a New 42-Space Eaton CH Panel

LPH will replace the existing Crouse-Hinds panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH panel. This provides a modern panel assembly with additional circuit spaces to help organize the home’s electrical system and accommodate future circuit additions, subject to the available service and load capacity.

The new panel will also provide a suitable platform for compatible circuit breakers and modern protective devices as needed for the home’s electrical requirements.

4. Improved Long-Term Reliability and Serviceability

Replacing the existing panel allows LPH to evaluate the incoming service conductors, grounding and bonding connections, neutral and ground terminations, and branch-circuit connections as part of the installation. This includes inspecting the breaker connections at the bus bar for looseness, signs of overheating, or other conditions that may affect safe operation. This helps identify concerns that may otherwise remain hidden within aging equipment.

A new panel can also make future electrical maintenance and troubleshooting more straightforward by providing current, compatible equipment and a more organized circuit layout.

5. Opportunity to Incorporate Whole-Home Surge Protection

As part of the panel replacement, LPH recommends installing whole-home surge protection to help protect sensitive electronics and appliances from damaging voltage transients originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, and electrical equipment cycling within the home.

Modern appliances and electronic equipment contain circuit boards and sensitive components that can be vulnerable to voltage surges. Whole-home surge protection provides an additional layer of defense for the home’s electrical system and connected equipment.

Scope of Work

LPH will:

* Remove the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while maintaining the existing 200-amp service rating, provided the existing service components and installation support that configuration.
* Transfer the existing branch circuits to the new panel using compatible circuit breakers and appropriate wiring methods.
* Inspect breaker connections at the bus bar and address any loose, damaged, or overheated connections identified during the installation.
* Inspect and address grounding, bonding, neutral, and equipment grounding connections as required for the installation.
* Verify circuit identification and organize the panel directory.
* Evaluate the existing service connections and associated components for any additional concerns identified during replacement.
* Test the completed installation to verify proper operation.
* Provide whole-home surge protection as a recommended additional upgrade, if included in the approved scope.

The Long-Term Benefit

Replacing the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is a proactive investment in the home’s electrical infrastructure. Rather than waiting for aging equipment to develop a problem, the homeowner can move forward with a modern panel that offers additional circuit spaces, improved serviceability, and a better foundation for future electrical upgrades.

The goal is not simply to replace a panel because it is old. It is to update an aging, critical electrical component so the home’s distribution system is better positioned to serve the family’s current needs and future electrical demands.

i.340570950:
LPH arrived at the residence to perform a comprehensive electrical system check evaluation throughout the home. The evaluation included inspecting the main electrical panel and subpanel, checking the condition of the breakers and visible electrical connections, evaluating grounding and bonding components, and looking for signs of corrosion, deterioration, overheating, or other potential electrical safety concerns.

LPH also tested accessible receptacles throughout the home, checked switches and electrical devices for proper operation, and inspected for loose devices and connections. A few loose electrical devices were tightened as LPH went around the home testing the receptacles. Accessible GFCI receptacles and their protective functions were checked where applicable, along with visible wiring conditions and the general condition of the home’s accessible electrical components.

Additional areas evaluated included accessible lighting fixtures and their operation, visible smoke and carbon monoxide detection equipment, exterior receptacles and weatherproof covers where accessible, and visible electrical connections and equipment throughout the home. LPH also looked for signs of damaged devices, improper installations, deterioration, and other conditions that could affect the safety or reliability of the electrical system. The remainder of the home’s accessible electrical components appeared to be in good working condition based on the evaluation performed.

During the evaluation, Gail reported noticeable voltage drops when new electrical loads begin drawing power. After tightening the panel connections, LPH applied pressure to the service cable wiring and could hear electrical arcing, with some circuits experiencing intermittent operation. These conditions raise serious concerns regarding the integrity of the existing electrical connections and the potential for overheating, equipment damage, or electrical failure.

The existing main electrical panel is approximately 45 years old and completely full, while the subpanel is nearly at capacity. Due to the age and condition of the equipment, the reported voltage fluctuations, and the audible arcing and intermittent circuit operation, LPH discussed replacing the existing main panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel and installing whole-home surge protection. A separate option for a complete 200 Amp underground electrical service replacement, including a new meter base and exterior emergency disconnect, was also discussed.

All findings and available options were reviewed with Gail, including the concerns identified with the existing electrical equipment and the benefits of the recommended upgrades. Gail would like approximately one week to review the options and determine how she would like to proceed.

LPH will follow up with Gail by phone in approximately one week to discuss her decision and determine the next steps. The estimates outlining the available options, along with today’s electrical system check evaluation, will be emailed to Gail for her review.

Thank you for allowing LPH into your home. We appreciate the opportunity to evaluate your electrical system and look forward to assisting you with your electrical needs in the future.

e.344497301:
200 Amp Underground Electrical Service Replacement

Reason for Replacement

The existing electrical service equipment has deteriorated significantly due to age, prolonged electrical loading, and the demands placed on the home’s electrical system. The main electrical panel is completely full, and the subpanel is also nearly at capacity, leaving limited room for additional circuits while placing continued demands on the existing equipment.

The homeowner has reported noticeable voltage drops when new electrical loads begin drawing power. During the electrical evaluation, LPH tightened the panel connections; however, when pressure was applied to the service cable wiring, electrical arcing could still be heard, and some circuits were observed experiencing intermittent operation.

These conditions are serious warning signs that the existing service connections and electrical distribution equipment may have deteriorated to the point where reliable electrical contact can no longer be assured. Loose or deteriorated connections can generate excessive heat and electrical arcing, potentially damaging equipment and increasing the risk of electrical failure or fire.

Due to the combination of noticeable voltage fluctuations, audible electrical arcing, intermittent circuit operation, deteriorated equipment, and heavily loaded panels, LPH recommends replacing the existing electrical service rather than continuing to rely on aging components. Simply tightening connections or replacing individual breakers would not adequately address the overall condition of the existing service equipment.

A complete service replacement will provide new service equipment, updated electrical distribution, improved circuit capacity, and a modernized grounding and bonding system to help restore reliable power delivery and reduce the risks associated with the deteriorated installation.

Scope of Work: 200 Amp Underground Electrical Service Upgrade

LPH will modernize the home’s electrical service by replacing the existing service equipment with a new 200 Amp system, including a new exterior emergency disconnect and a new interior electrical panel.

Scope of Work Includes:

* Remove the existing deteriorated electrical panel and associated service equipment.
* Install a new 200 Amp meter base.
* Replace the underground service entrance conductors and associated connections as required by the approved scope and utility requirements.
* Install a new exterior 200 Amp emergency disconnect to provide an accessible means of shutting off power to the home during an emergency or when servicing the electrical system.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel.
* Transfer and properly terminate existing branch circuits in the new panel.
* Install new breakers throughout the panel as required for the existing circuits.
* Properly separate neutral and grounding conductors within the new panel.
* Upgrade the grounding and bonding system to meet applicable electrical code requirements.
* Install top-tier whole-home surge protection at the new electrical panel.
* Install protective conduit for exterior service conductors where applicable to protect against physical damage and environmental exposure.
* Properly seal applicable service entry points to help prevent moisture intrusion.
* Label the new electrical panel and individual circuits.
* Inspect and verify electrical connections, terminations, grounding, and bonding.
* Coordinate required permits, inspections, and PPL scheduling as applicable.
* Test the completed installation and verify proper operation of the electrical system.

Why a Complete Replacement Is Recommended

1. Addressing Electrical Arcing and Intermittent Power

Audible arcing when pressure is applied to the service cable wiring, combined with circuits intermittently going in and out, indicates a potentially hazardous connection or equipment failure. Electrical arcing can produce intense localized heat, damage conductors and terminals, and increase the risk of an electrical fire. These conditions warrant prompt corrective action.

2. Correcting Voltage Fluctuations Under Load

Noticeable voltage drops when new electrical loads start can indicate excessive voltage drop, deteriorated connections, inadequate conductors, or another supply-side or distribution problem. A complete service replacement will allow the affected service components and connections to be replaced, although the underlying cause of the voltage fluctuations must be verified rather than assumed.

3. Replacing Deteriorated Electrical Equipment

The existing equipment has experienced decades of service and prolonged electrical loading. Aging breakers, bus connections, and terminations can deteriorate over time. Replacing the existing panel and service equipment will establish a new foundation for dependable electrical distribution rather than continuing to rely on components showing signs of deterioration.

4. Improving Electrical Capacity and Organization

The main panel is completely full, and the subpanel is nearly full. The new 42-space Eaton CH panel will provide additional circuit spaces and a modernized distribution arrangement. The new 200 Amp service will also provide greater capacity where supported by the home’s calculated electrical load and the utility service.

5. Adding an Exterior Emergency Disconnect

The new exterior emergency disconnect will provide an accessible means of disconnecting power to the home. This improves accessibility for emergency response and servicing while modernizing the home’s service equipment.

6. Protecting Connected Electronics and Appliances

The new whole-home surge protective device will help protect sensitive electronics, appliances, and other connected equipment from damaging voltage surges caused by lightning, utility disturbances, and other electrical events.

Underground Service Protection and Longevity

The new service equipment will be installed with appropriate protection and sealing to help minimize exposure to physical damage and moisture intrusion. Exterior service conductors will be installed in protective conduit where applicable to the installation and utility requirements.

Replacing the service connections, meter base, exterior emergency disconnect, and interior electrical panel will address the major components included in this service replacement and help establish a more reliable electrical infrastructure for the home.

Peace-of-Mind Warranty

The new Eaton CH electrical panel and breakers are protected by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while the homeowner maintains an active LPH Service Partner Plan (SPP) membership, providing continued coverage and additional peace of mind.

Long-Term Value

This project is more than a routine electrical panel replacement. It addresses documented concerns involving voltage fluctuations, audible arcing, intermittent circuit operation, aging service equipment, and limited panel capacity.

By replacing the existing service equipment, installing a new exterior emergency disconnect, upgrading grounding and bonding, and adding whole-home surge protection, LPH will help address the conditions affecting the home’s electrical reliability while providing a modernized 200 Amp electrical service designed to support the home’s needs for years to come.

All work will be completed in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements and the requirements of the serving utility and local authority having jurisdiction.
e.344577972:
Electrical Panel Replacement & Whole-Home Surge Protection

Reason for Replacement

The existing electrical panel has been in service for approximately 45 years and is showing signs of deterioration after decades of electrical loading. The main panel is completely full, and the subpanel is nearly at capacity, leaving limited room for additional circuits and future electrical upgrades.

The homeowner has reported noticeable voltage drops when new electrical loads begin drawing power. During the electrical evaluation, LPH tightened the panel connections; however, when pressure was applied to the service cable wiring, audible electrical arcing could still be heard, and some circuits were observed experiencing intermittent operation.

These symptoms raise serious concerns regarding the condition of the existing electrical connections and distribution equipment. Deteriorated connections can create excessive resistance, localized overheating, and electrical arcing, potentially damaging equipment and increasing the risk of electrical failure or fire.

Due to the age and condition of the existing equipment, the audible arcing, intermittent circuit operation, and limited panel capacity, LPH recommends replacing the existing electrical panel rather than continuing to rely on deteriorated components. Simply tightening connections or replacing individual breakers may not adequately address the overall condition of the existing panel.

Scope of Work Includes:

* Remove the existing approximately 45-year-old electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel.
* Transfer and properly terminate the existing branch circuits in the new panel.
* Install new breakers throughout the panel as required for the existing circuits.
* Properly separate neutral and grounding conductors within the panel as required.
* Inspect and verify electrical connections, terminations, and grounding.
* Install top-tier whole-home surge protection at the new electrical panel.
* Properly label the new panel and individual circuits.
* Test the completed installation and verify proper operation of the electrical system.

Benefits of Replacing the Existing Panel

Improved Electrical Safety: Replacing the aging panel and associated breakers addresses deterioration within the existing distribution equipment. New equipment and properly completed terminations help reduce the risks associated with worn components and unreliable electrical connections.

Addressing Arcing and Intermittent Circuits: The reported arcing and intermittent circuit operation are significant warning signs that require attention. Replacing the panel provides an opportunity to inspect and properly reconnect the existing branch circuits and evaluate the affected connections. Any damaged service conductors or other components outside the panel replacement scope may require additional repairs.

Improved Power Reliability: A new panel and properly terminated connections can help resolve problems caused by deteriorated panel components or connections. However, because voltage fluctuations can also originate from the service conductors, utility supply, or other parts of the electrical system, further investigation may be necessary if the symptoms persist.

Additional Circuit Capacity: The new 42-space Eaton CH panel provides additional breaker spaces, improving circuit organization and allowing greater flexibility for future electrical additions. The existing subpanel and the home’s overall electrical load will still need to be considered when planning future upgrades.

Whole-Home Surge Protection: LPH will install a whole-home surge protective device to help protect sensitive electronics, appliances, and other connected equipment from damaging voltage surges caused by lightning, utility disturbances, and other electrical events.

Peace-of-Mind Warranty

The new Eaton CH electrical panel and breakers are protected by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while maintaining an active LPH Service Partner Plan (SPP) membership, providing continued coverage and added peace of mind.

Long-Term Value

Replacing the existing electrical panel will modernize a critical part of the home’s electrical infrastructure while addressing concerns associated with aging equipment, limited circuit capacity, and potentially deteriorated connections.

The new Eaton CH panel, properly terminated branch circuits, and whole-home surge protection will provide an improved foundation for electrical safety, reliability, and future circuit additions.

Important Note: This option covers the electrical panel replacement and whole-home surge protection only. It does not include replacement of the underground electrical service, meter base, or exterior service equipment. If the source of the voltage fluctuations or arcing is found to involve the incoming service conductors or equipment outside the panel, additional repairs or a complete service replacement may be necessary.

All work will be completed in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements and the requirements of the local authority having jurisdiction.

e.343982375:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 16 grains per gallon. A hardness level of 16 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, shower heads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a cabinet water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the washer connecting to the washer drain. Technician will have to open up the drywall. at the proposed installation area. The system also requires a dedicated electrical outlet for operation and regeneration cycles. An outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

i.341115614: This morning I arrived at the Radanovic family home to perfrom their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon my arrival Mr. Radanovic informed me he only wanted me to check his main service. I found only one discrepancy which was a shared neutral in the sub panel. Two separate circuits using one neutral can lead to an overload of the neutral. This overloading can cause damage, burning, or loss of neutral connection. IF this neutral were to lose its connection, the two circuits remaining energized could overload with no exit path and become potentially 240v circuits, destroying any appliances or equipment not rated to handle that much voltage. I have provided an option to replace these two circuits with an appropriate double pole breaker. That is my only recommendation for today. If you have any questions or concerns please do not hesitate to reach out. Thank you.

i.341124358:
This afternoon I arrived at the Rivera family home for their complimentary system check, and to address concerns regarding a tripping circuit. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service I found it to be a roughly 40+ year old Crouse & Hinds 100A panel. The panel only has a small amount of available space remaining with tandem breakers being our only opportunity for edition in the panels current state. I found that the home has 5 window units which at times are all operating at once, this is absolutely grounds for causing a circuit to trip, especially with other electronics plugged into this same circuit. I am providing 3 options today, with one being a combination of the two in a bundle. 

The first option I will be providing is to install two tandem 20A breakers on our last available breakers available, and then to drill outside the home to run PVC conduit up the sides of the house to both the front bedroom window, and then the bedroom in the back alley between the homes. From there we will drill back into the house underneath the window where we will install a single outlet to shed the load for two window units on that circuit. 

The second option I will be providing is a full service upgrade. This option consists of replacing the entire main electrical service consisting of breaker panel, and outdoor meterbase and service wiring which runs through the roof of the porch and into the basement breaker panel. This option will include removing active fuse box circuits and incorporating them into the panel. 

The final option I will be providing is a bundle of both of these projects at once. In doing all of the work at once you are eligible for savings on the total project cost.

I have provided a copy of our companies membership during todays visit, this membership comes with a built in 15% discount which will be shown as potential savings within the provided estimates.

If you have any questions regarding these estimates, or concerns, please do not hesitate to reach out. Thank you for your time and we look forward to our next visit.

i.341545395: This morning I arrived at the Harrison family home for their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon performing a thorough evaluation of the homes main electrical service I found no major discrepancies. However, Mrs. Harrison informed me that they have had a history of blowing the fuses that supply power to their hot water heater. After performing an analysis of the system I noted several things. First, and most importantly, I noted that the wire which supplies power to the disconnect is undersized. The water heater requires a 30A (amp) supply in order to properly function. The wire which is currently in use is only rated AT MOST to handle 20A. The heater, the disconnect itself, and the breaker are all designed for a 30A load, where as the wiring, which acts as the bridge for all of these systems is only designed for 20A. Secondly, the Harrisons have been using 20A replacement fuses for this 30A system which is why they have been blowing with such frequency. Unfortunately, stepping the fuses up to 30A could become a potential fire hazard with the wire unable to handle that load. If 30A fuses are installed, that wire may burn and become damaged well before that fuse would ever blow. I have some indication of potential heat as it seems the ends of the stripped insulation on the hot wires has begun to soften and partially deform. I encouraged the Harrisons to continue to use these 20A fuses until they are able to replace the system. While they may blow more frequently, it is all that can be done until we replace the wiring, which is imperative. I have provided two options. The first which is most recommended would consist of replace the disconnect with a modern electrical disconnect requiring no fuses, and to replace the wire. The second option would be to replace the wire solely to avoid potential overheating. If you have any questions or if you would like to move forward with these options, please do not hesitate to reach out. Thank you, and we will see you in our next visit!

Premium Whole-Home Surge Protection
LPH will install a premium whole-home surge protection device at the home’s main electrical panel. This device is designed to protect the home’s electrical system and connected equipment from damaging voltage spikes and transient surges before they can travel throughout the home’s wiring.
Many homeowners think of lightning when they hear the term “surge,” but the majority of power surges actually originate inside the home. Everyday appliances such as air conditioners, refrigerators, heat pumps, furnaces, microwaves, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and even garage door openers create small electrical surges—known as microsurges—every time their motors cycle on and off. While each individual surge is small, thousands of these microsurges occur over time and gradually wear down the sensitive electronic components found in today’s modern appliances and equipment.
Whole-home surge protection helps absorb and divert these surges away from the home’s electrical system, reducing cumulative damage to expensive electronics and appliances. This is especially important in newer homes, where nearly every major appliance contains sophisticated circuit boards and microprocessors that are far more sensitive to voltage fluctuations than older equipment.
In addition to protecting against internally generated microsurges, whole-home surge protection also provides a critical first line of defense against larger surges originating from the utility company, switching events on the electrical grid, nearby lightning strikes, or power being restored after an outage.
Benefits of premium whole-home surge protection include:
	• Protects HVAC systems, refrigerators, ovens, dishwashers, washers, dryers, and other major appliances.
	• Helps safeguard sensitive electronics such as televisions, computers, gaming systems, networking equipment, and smart home devices.
	• Reduces the long-term effects of everyday microsurges that slowly degrade electronic components.
	• Can help extend the service life of modern appliances and equipment by reducing electrical stress on internal circuit boards.
	• Helps minimize the likelihood of costly repairs or premature equipment replacement due to surge damage.
	• Provides continuous protection for the entire home’s electrical system without relying solely on individual plug-in surge strips.
	• Offers added peace of mind during storms, utility switching events, and unexpected power outages.
As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

Premium Surge Protection Warranty & Replacement Coverage

The installed surge protection device also provides additional protection beyond the device itself. If the surge protector is ever sacrificed or fails as a result of a covered surge event, the device is backed by a lifetime warranty and coverage of up to $100,000 toward covered damage to the home’s electrical components and connected equipment, subject to the manufacturer’s warranty terms and conditions.

If the surge protector ever needs to be replaced under the warranty, the replacement device is provided at no charge. LPH will also handle the replacement installation for a $150 labor charge, helping make future warranty replacement straightforward and affordable for the homeowner.

This means the homeowner is not simply purchasing a surge protector—they are adding a long-term layer of protection to the home’s electrical system while also having manufacturer-backed coverage in the event of a significant surge.

As homes continue to rely on more connected technology and electronically controlled appliances, whole-home surge protection has become one of the most valuable upgrades for preserving the reliability, longevity, and performance of a home’s electrical equipment.

i.341685691:
This estimate includes having Lancaster Plumbing and Heating make a warranty repair on the water softener. It would include removal of the mechanical parts of the head that control the stages of the water softeners regeneration. This repair is covered under both the manufacturer’s parts warranty and Lancaster Plumbing and Heating’s labor warranty.

We came out today to take a look at the water softener because it was showing an error code. The error code was indicating that there was a motor failure. This usually means that during regeneration the computer was telling the spacer stack assembly to switch positions and it took too long or got stuck.

The technician began diagnosing the issue by disconnecting power and trying a hard reset of the electrical components. This did not fix the issue, so the technician provided an estimate to perform a warranty repair. The warranty repair included replacing the spacer stack assembly, and the motor that drives the functions for the spacer stack assembly. Once the repair was completed, the technician put the water softener through an abbreviated regeneration twice in order to verify that the system was now working properly. Both attempts on the abbreviated regeneration were successful and everything was in proper operation at this time.

The technician did discover a secondary issue, but it had to do with the Brian tank. The homeowners have been using salt pellets instead of salt crystals, and this is caused bridging within the brine tank. The technician suggested that the salt be dug out of the brine tank in order to fix this issue. Moving forward we did recommend the use of salt crystals because they do dissolve easier with these particular systems.

If you have any other questions or concerns that arise after today’s visit, please do not hesitate to give us a call. Thank you for continuing to trust Lancaster Plumbing and Heating with all of your home service needs. 
This estimate includes having Lancaster Plumbing and Heating unload the brine tank in order to remove a large chunk of salt pellets.

A technician was dispatched today after the homeowner reported hearing the booster pump activate when no water was being used. The homeowner stated that this issue has been occurring intermittently for several months. Upon inspection, the technician checked the unit’s air bladder pressure and confirmed that it was at the proper level. All plumbing fixtures, including toilets and faucets, were inspected to ensure there were no visible drips or leaks. No error codes were present on the unit, and the system correctly indicated when the pump was operating and when it was in standby mode. The homeowner mentioned that he had replaced a toilet flapper several weeks ago. A possible cause of the issue is that the toilet flapper is not sealing properly, allowing water to slowly leak into the bowl and causing the toilet to periodically refill. This could trigger the booster pump to activate even when no other water is being used. The technician monitored the system for at least 15 minutes while downstairs to verify that the pump did not activate unexpectedly. During this observation period, the pump operated as expected and did not cycle on randomly.nAt the time of inspection, the system was functioning properly, and no issues were found with the booster pump or its air bladder.
