The homeowner requested that the heat tape and insulation under the mobile home be inspected. The homeowner has lived at the residence for approximately 17 years and has not experienced any issues with the water lines freezing.

Technician tested the electrical outlet supplying the heat tape and verified that the outlet is properly grounded and operating correctly. During the inspection, Technician observed that the water main is currently wrapped with approximately 1/8-inch-thick Seal Seal foam insulation, which is typically used for foundation applications. This insulation provides minimal protection against freezing temperatures.

Technician recommends replacing the existing insulation on the water main with 1/2-inch to 1-inch-thick pipe insulation to provide additional protection from freezing temperatures. Approximately 25 feet of insulation would be required to properly insulate the exposed water main.

Technician also recommends insulating the pit where the water main enters the mobile home from below grade. Regular R-19 insulation should be installed around the pit to help retain heat and provide additional protection for the water main during freezing temperatures.

i.341956738:
LPH arrived to begin the annual electrical system check. Upon arrival, Jason reported some concerns and project ideas for this home. We were informed that Jason wanted options for new panels to be installed to replace the existing main and sub panel. Jason also wanted an option to install all new washer and dryer receptacles in the garage for easier accessibility. 

We began our evaluation at the main electrical/distribution panel. This is where we assessed the internal conditions, age, connections and voltage readings. During this inspection, most of the inspected parameters meet the required threshold for a healthy panel. However, there are a few recommendations we assessed during this inspection. 

First we discovered that these panels are the Zinsco brand, which is a brand that lost their UL listing many years ago and is no longer allowed to be installed. This brand along, with two other brands that have similar issues, no longer have any replacement parts or breakers available. Second we noticed that this electrical system is currently within the “end of life” range, which means the longevity is in question. Lastly, there’s no system put in place to protect appliances/electronics from spikes of electric which target the sensitive components inside these units. A whole home surge protection device is recommended if the homeowners were interested in  protecting their main utility equipment with a one time investment unit.

Next, we inspected all of the protective systems for personnel and equipment in the home such as the smoke detectors, GFI protection devices, and the grounding system. First, we discovered that the water meter does not meet today’s grounding standards to protect against any leakage of electricity from traveling on the pipes. The next was identifying that all of the existing smoke detectors and carbon monoxide detectors are either not currently installed or past their 10 year lifespan. Lastly, we identified multiple areas with missing GFI protection, which is the bathroom, the washer in the basement, kitchen and exterior. All other devices in the home were tested and functioning properly prior to leaving today.

We provided options to remedy all of our electrical recommendations, which was presented today. All of the options that were not approved will be emailed along with the electrical evaluation form and invoice for today’s visit. We thank you for allowing us in your home to service you and we look forward to servicing you in the future.

We were called out to provide options to remedy any power loss concern for Evan and his family. Upon arrival, we spoke with Evan, who informed us of what exactly he was looking for in portable generators systems, and wanted some clarity on some information that he researched on his own time. After speaking with Evan, we got a great understanding of what he was looking for to be installed in this home and for length of the time that he planned on staying in this home. We were looking to install a new 50 amp plug on the exterior of the home with a twist lock style receptacle, a new 50 amp breaker that will be protected and controlled by an interlock kit that will fit this panel cover exactly. We also looked at the outdoor unit to assess the amperage/wattage usage and noticed that it will work with the two generators that Evan was looking into(8,500W or 11,000W). However, we did inform Evan that if he went with the 8.5 KW style generator, he would be very limited in total usage after the outdoor unit, freezer, and well pump were under use.

i.342391384: This afternoon I arrived at the Mitchell family home to conduct their annual electrical system and safety check. Upon my arrival, Mr. Mitchell informed me of some concerns related to the location of his breaker panel. Upon performing an inspection I found the breaker panel to be located in the downstairs bathroom. According to NEC revision 1993, breaker panels are not allowed to be located in any bathroom facilities, The code defines a bathroom (Article 100) as any area including a basin (sink) with one or more fixtures like a toilet, tub, or shower. Even a half-bath or powder room with just a sink and a toilet legally meets this definition. Therefore, overcurrent devices and service panels are still forbidden under NEC 240.24(E). For this reason, I have built the Mitchell’s an option to relocate their main electrical panel to a separate location in the basement outside the bathroom, and away from other water piping related systems. Otherwise I presented several other estimates regarding some code compliance features in the home. Ultimately I found the main electrical systems to be in goof physical condition with no signs of deterioration. If you have any questions or concerns related to todays visit, please do not hesitate to reach out! Thank you for having us out today and I look forward to our next visit!

Date: 10/8 9-4

i.342862190:
Technician investigated concerns of sewer gas odor entering the main-floor master bathroom shower area and laundry room. Technician checked the water level in the master bathroom shower drain and inspected the 3” vent termination through the roof, which is located directly above the master bathroom. The 3” vent was found to extend approximately 6–8” above the roof.

Technician explained that windy conditions can create a Venturi effect at the vent termination, potentially drawing air through the vent system and affecting the water seal in the shower P-trap. Wind can also create direct downdrafts through the vent, which may contribute to sewer gas odors entering the home. Technician discussed raising the existing vent termination and adding a U-bend configuration using two 3” 90° fittings to help reduce the potential for wind-driven downdrafts.

Technician also recommended installing a 2” Trap Guard in the shower drain. The Trap Guard allows water to drain normally while providing an additional barrier to help prevent sewer gas from entering the home if the P-trap water seal is compromised.

The main-floor laundry room is equipped with two laundry drains, each with a 2” P-trap. One of the drains is not regularly used, and the water in the P-trap may be evaporating and allowing sewer gas to enter the laundry room. The unused drain will either be used for the dehumidifier discharge to maintain the P-trap water seal or capped to prevent sewer gas from entering through the drain.

The homeowner plans to purchase a trap guard before addressing the vent through the roof.

We were called out today because of a leak that was discovered at the geothermal pre-heating water tank. Upon arrival Rachel briefed the technician about the leak that was discovered and then took the technician down to the basement to see exactly what was going on. As the technician began inspection the the tank and surrounding area, it was quickly determined that the leak wasn’t going to be repairable. The leak itself is coming from the tank, and not a part or water line connected to the tank. After sharing this info with the home the technician did discuss a couple of options that could be done moving forward, but wanted to speak with the field supervisor about what would be best. Before the technician was able to go over the estimates completely, Rachel had to depart for a scheduled doctor’s appointment. The technician finished the estimates and was able to email them over in order for Rachel to look at while she was in the waiting room at her appointment.

This estimate includes having Lancaster Plumbing and Heating replace the standard electric water heater with a hybrid water heater. In addition we would also remove, properly dispose of the existing geothermal pre-heating water tank and cap the existing water lines.

Once our estimate was approved, we went to work with removal of the existing tanks. Before draining the water heaters down, we did have to figure out how to disable the research pump for the existing geothermal preheating tank. After some back-and-forth with our HVAC managers and doing some research, we discovered that we could disconnect the pump from its power source and in doing so would not interrupt The heating aspect of the geothermal system. Once the new water heater was in, we restored water to the home and began filling out the tank. Once the tank was filled, we were able to inspect all new connections to ensure everything was flowing properly and water tight. The Weber’s were extremely happy with the effort we put in today and with the final look of the install.

If you have any other questions or concerns that arise after today’s visit, please do not hesitate to give us a call. Thank you for continuing to trust Lancaster Plumbing and Heating with all of your home service needs.

A Moen Flo is a smart water monitoring and leak-detection system for your home. It’s designed to help prevent expensive water damage from leaking pipes, broken hoses, running toilets, or burst plumbing.
What does a Moen Flo do?
1. Detects leaks
Monitors the water flowing through your home's main water line.
Learns your household's normal water-use patterns.
Can detect unusual water flow that may indicate a leak.
2. Automatically shuts off your water
If it detects a serious leak or abnormal water use, it can automatically turn off your home's main water supply to help prevent flooding.
You can also shut the water off remotely using the app, depending on your setup.
3. Monitors water usage
Shows how much water your household uses.
Can help identify unusual usage, such as a toilet that keeps running.
4. Sends alerts to your phone
- Notifies you about possible leaks, unusual water use, and other problems.
Moen says its system can detect some leaks as small as one drop per minute. It needs to be properly installed and configured, and it isn't a guarantee against all water damage.

Technician performed a thorough plumbing system inspection on all accessible plumbing fixtures throughout the home to evaluate overall operation, drainage, water flow, and visible plumbing conditions. During the inspection, technician identified a few concerns within the plumbing system and discussed recommended solutions with the homeowner to address the issues found. Technician reviewed available repair and improvement options to help maintain proper system performance and prevent future plumbing problems.

e.344279558:
The trip lever/tub stopper in the 2nd-floor hallway bathroom bathtub is not functioning because the existing lever is broken. The bathtub is equipped with a PVC Watco waste and overflow assembly. Technician recommends replacing the broken trip lever with a new PVC Watco trip lever compatible with the existing waste and overflow assembly. This will restore proper operation of the bathtub stopper, allowing the stopper to open and close as intended for filling and draining the bathtub.

The existing second-floor hallway bathroom toilet is a standard-height, round-bowl toilet that is older and outdated. Technician recommends replacing the existing toilet with a new comfort-height, elongated-bowl toilet. The comfort-height design provides added comfort and ease of use, while the elongated bowl offers additional seating space. The new toilet will also use less water per flush, helping improve water efficiency and reduce overall water consumption. Technician will remove the existing toilet, install the new toilet with a new wax ring and supply connection as needed, and test the toilet to ensure proper flushing, filling, and operation with no leaks.

During the annual plumbing system check, Technician noticed that the main-floor kitchen sink drain gurgles when draining. Technician inspected the kitchen sink drainage system and found that the drain is not properly vented. Improper venting can restrict airflow within the drainage system, causing gurgling noises and potentially affecting the drain’s ability to discharge wastewater properly. Technician recommends installing an air admittance valve (AAV) on the kitchen sink drain to provide the necessary airflow and help maintain proper drainage. This will help equalize pressure within the drain piping, reduce gurgling noises, and allow wastewater to drain more efficiently. Technician will install the air admittance valve in an accessible location and test the kitchen sink drain to verify proper operation.

During the plumbing system inspection, Technician noticed that the existing sump pump pit is not equipped with a sump pump. Water was present inside the pit, indicating that groundwater is entering the sump pit and that the basement may be susceptible to groundwater accumulation and potential flooding. Technician recommends installing a new sump pump in the existing pit to help remove accumulated groundwater and reduce the risk of basement flooding and potential water damage.

The sump pump discharge piping would be installed to direct water from the pump to the exterior of the home. The discharge line would terminate approximately 25 feet away at the rear of the house, running along the basement stairwell and extending beyond the end of the stairwell to direct water away from the foundation. A designated electrical outlet would need to be provided to supply power to the new sump pump. Once installed, Technician will test the sump pump and discharge system to verify proper operation and confirm that water is being pumped away from the home.

This is to do a sewer line replacement from the trap on the inside of the basement to the curb. LPH would use an excavating machine to expose the existing compromised pipe. Once the compromised pipe is located, LPH will remove it and then lay a bed of crushed stone down. Once the sewer line is exposed, LPH will remove it and then lay down a bed of crushed stone. LPH will then start to connect the new scheduled 40 PVC sewer line. Once the sewer line is connected, LPH will use hydraulic cement on the inside and outside foundation wall. Another bed of crushed stone will be placed on top of the PVC pipe and backfill will begin. Backfill will be tamped to a raked finish. The homeowner is responsible to finish the landscaping. The concrete in the basement will be completed to a smooth finish. The sidewalk out front will be filled with crushed stone until we finish the concrete (weather permitting). The concrete is included in this estimate. The trap will be relocated to the outside of the home. Once we have the pipe cut at the curb, we will perform a video inspection from the curb to the main. This estimate includes having Lancaster Plumbing and Heating clear a blockage at the kitchen sink. It will involve disassembling the tubular PVC drain piping from the food waste disposer down to the p-trap.

We came out today because of a leak leak and back up at the food waste disposer. Upon arrival, the homeowners explained what was going on when they discovered the issue which allowed the technician quickly determine what the issue was. The technician discovered that the locking collar for the equipment was not locked in place, and in addition determined that that side of the double bay sink was backed up. 

After further discussion, the technician learned that there were certain things going into the disposer that shouldn’t have been. We also learned that too much food was going down at one time. An estimate was provided to take apart the center drain outlet in order to clear the blockage. Upon disassembling the drain, we did discover a large quantity of food between the first section of drain piping and the second fitting that attaches to the P-trap. We were able to quickly get the blockage clear and the drain piping reassembled. Once everything was back together, the technician tested everything to ensure there were zero leaks and proper flow.

We did provide an estimate to install a customer supplied food waste disposer and to also replace the center drain outlet piping. We are not saying that there needs to be an immediate replacement. This would be a preventative maintenance replacement due to the amount of rust we saw at the locking collar. We also don’t know the condition of the rubber gasket that creates a water tight seal. At this time, everything was in proper operation and leak free.

If you have any other questions or concerns that arise after today’s visit, please do not hesitate to give us a call. Thank you for continuing to trust Lancaster Plumbing and Heating with all of your home service needs.

Home Surge protection protections your home from any surges that may occur in the home. 20 percent of surges come from outside the home such as a surge from the power company or stray lighting strikes. e.344275829:
When flushing the toilet in the main floor hallway bathroom, a gurgling sound can be heard coming from the bathtub drain. This may indicate an issue with the existing drain and venting configuration. Upon inspection, the existing bathtub drain consists of 1-1/2” copper piping connected to an S-trap configuration, which is not properly vented and can interfere with the drainage system’s ability to maintain proper airflow. When the toilet is flushed, the sudden discharge of water through the drainage system can create pressure fluctuations that may cause air to be pulled through the bathtub trap, resulting in the gurgling sound. Improper venting can also affect the bathtub trap seal, potentially allowing sewer gases to enter the home if the water seal is compromised. The home’s main plumbing vent is supplied from the top of the main waste stack.

Technician recommends replacing the existing 1-1/2” copper bathtub drain piping with 2” PVC piping and replacing the corroded brass bathtub waste and overflow assembly. This will provide updated drain piping and a new waste and overflow assembly while allowing the existing drain configuration to be evaluated and corrected as needed. Technician will assess the existing S-trap arrangement and determine the appropriate corrections to improve drainage and provide proper venting in accordance with applicable plumbing code requirements.

Technician also recommends inspecting the plumbing vent through the roof to check for possible obstructions, such as debris or other blockages, that could restrict airflow through the vent system. A restricted vent can contribute to gurgling sounds, slow drainage, and improper pressure balance within the plumbing system. Clearing any obstructions found may help restore proper airflow. These recommended repairs and inspections are intended to improve drainage performance, reduce the gurgling sound when flushing the toilet, and help maintain the proper water seal in the bathtub drain trap. Additional venting modifications may be necessary depending on the existing plumbing configuration and the findings during the repair.

e.345022885:
Technician performed water quality testing and found the home’s water hardness to be 19 grains per gallon (GPG) and the chlorine level to be 1.0 ppm. A hardness level of 19 GPG is considered hard water and can lead to calcium and magnesium scale buildup inside water heaters, plumbing fixtures, faucets, showerheads, and water-using appliances. Over time, this mineral buildup can reduce appliance efficiency, shorten equipment life expectancy, cause spotting on dishes and glassware, and leave soap residue on fixtures and surfaces. The presence of chlorine, while common in municipal water supplies, can contribute to dry skin and hair and may deteriorate rubber seals and gaskets within the plumbing system over time.

To improve water quality and help protect the home’s plumbing system, technician recommends installing a City Soft water treatment system. The system is designed to soften the water by removing the hardness minerals that cause scale buildup while also reducing chlorine levels throughout the home. Benefits of the system include improved soap and detergent performance, reduced spotting and scaling, softer-feeling water, and increased protection and efficiency of plumbing fixtures and water-using appliances.

The proposed installation location for the City Soft system is near the existing water heater to allow for efficient integration into the home’s main water distribution system. The softener’s backwash drain lines will be routed and connected to the existing main drain located behind the water heater at the proposed installation area. An outlet is provided. Once installed, the system will provide conditioned water to the entire home and help minimize the long-term effects of hard water and chlorine exposure on the plumbing system.

e.344691385:
Electrical Panel Replacement – Crouse-Hinds Panel

Reason for Replacement

LPH recommends replacing the existing 42-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel due to its age and visible signs of deterioration. The panel has exceeded its typical service life, and several concerning conditions were identified during the electrical evaluation.

Signs of rust were observed on several breakers, along with heat discoloration above the main breaker. These conditions can indicate deterioration and potential overheating within the electrical panel. Additionally, the original breakers were noticeably loose in their connections. When the breakers were gently moved, a light amount of electrical arcing could be heard, raising concerns about the integrity of the breaker-to-bus connections and the potential for unreliable electrical contact.

As electrical panels and their components age, connections can loosen, contact surfaces can deteriorate, and corrosion can develop. These conditions can increase electrical resistance, generate excessive heat, and contribute to electrical arcing. If left unaddressed, deteriorated connections can damage the panel and breakers while increasing the potential for electrical failure or fire.

Due to the age of the panel, rust on the breakers, heat discoloration, and audible arcing associated with movement of the original breakers, LPH recommends replacing the existing electrical panel rather than continuing to rely on deteriorated equipment.

Installing a new electrical panel will provide modern electrical distribution equipment, new breakers, and properly established connections to improve the safety and reliability of the home’s electrical system.

Scope of Work Includes:

* Remove the existing 42-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel.
* Transfer and properly terminate the existing branch circuits.
* Install new breakers appropriate for the existing circuits and new panel.
* Inspect existing branch-circuit wiring for signs of damage or deterioration at accessible connection points.
* Properly establish neutral and grounding connections in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements.
* Inspect and verify electrical terminations and connections.
* Properly label the new electrical panel and individual circuits.
* Test the completed installation and verify proper operation of the electrical system.

Benefits of Replacing the Existing Panel

Improved Electrical Safety: Replacing the aging panel addresses concerns associated with deteriorated equipment, rust, heat discoloration, and loose breaker connections. New equipment and properly established connections help reduce the risks associated with overheating and electrical arcing.

Reliable Breaker Connections: The original breakers have become noticeably loose, and movement produced audible arcing. A new panel with compatible breakers will provide new breaker mounting and contact components, helping establish reliable electrical connections.

Reduced Risk of Overheating: Rust and heat discoloration are warning signs that warrant attention. Replacing the panel allows the affected equipment to be removed and the connected wiring to be inspected for damage before being terminated in the new panel.

Modern Electrical Distribution: A new 42-space Eaton CH panel provides a modern electrical distribution system designed to accommodate compatible breakers and support the home’s electrical needs.

Future Electrical Flexibility: The new panel provides additional circuit spaces for potential future electrical additions, subject to the available service capacity and the home’s calculated electrical load.

Peace-of-Mind Warranty

Your new Eaton CH electrical panel and breakers are protected by a 10-year parts and labor warranty while maintaining an active LPH Service Partner Plan (SPP) membership, providing continued coverage and added peace of mind.

Long-Term Value

Replacing the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is a proactive investment in the safety and reliability of the home’s electrical system. With the panel approximately 42 years old and showing signs of rust, heat discoloration, loose breaker connections, and audible arcing, continuing to rely on the existing equipment presents avoidable concerns.

A new electrical panel will replace the deteriorated components, provide properly established breaker connections, and help restore dependable electrical distribution throughout the home.

All work will be completed in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements and the requirements of the local authority having jurisdiction.

i.344498603:
Homeowner showed the technician the condensation pump located in the basement at the Bosch furnace installed by LPH. Homeowner explained that the condensation pump had been experiencing intermittent issues with turning on and/or keeping up with the amount of condensation being produced. During these occurrences, the thermostat would display an error indicating that the system was waiting for the unit. LPH previously replaced the thermostat twice without resolving the issue. LPH also replaced the condensation pump twice; however, the problem continued to occur, most recently the previous week while the air conditioning system was running.

Technician connected a hose to the boiler drain at the well pressure tank to introduce water into the condensation pump and simulate the drainage from two units running simultaneously. During testing, technician observed that the condensation pump was discharging water too slowly to keep up with the incoming water flow. Technician inspected the existing 3/8-inch PEX discharge tubing and determined that it was restricting the discharge flow. Technician replaced the existing 3/8-inch PEX tubing with 3/8-inch vinyl tubing. After replacing the tubing, technician tested the condensation pump again and observed improved water flow and a faster discharge rate. This correction improved the pump’s ability to remove water during testing.

Due to the ongoing nature of this issue and the previous attempts to resolve it, technician waived the dispatch fee and completed the discharge tubing replacement at no additional charge.

e.344707129:
LPH will install a new, dedicated electrical circuit from the electrical panel to the location where the oxygen pump is stationed. The oxygen pump is currently causing nuisance tripping of the brand-new arc-fault circuit breaker, which was previously replaced in September after similar issues began following the delivery of a new machine to the home.

The concern is that the oxygen pump may be contributing to the issue in two ways: the possibility of overloading the existing shared circuit with other electrical devices, or electrical interference generated by the pump’s internal condenser and electronic components that may be triggering the arc-fault breaker’s sensitive detection circuitry after approximately one hour of operation.

Installing a dedicated circuit will separate the oxygen pump from other electrical loads and help eliminate concerns associated with sharing the existing circuit. Using a standard circuit breaker, where permitted by applicable electrical code and the equipment manufacturer’s requirements, will also help address potential nuisance tripping associated with the pump’s electronic operation.

This solution is intended to provide a more reliable power source for the oxygen pump, reduce the likelihood of unexpected interruptions, and provide the homeowner with greater peace of mind when relying on this equipment.

Technician snaked the laundry and kitchen drain due to slow drainage and the presence of an existing underground cast-iron drain line. To help improve drainage and reduce the potential for future blockages associated with the existing underground piping, Technician recommends rerouting the laundry and kitchen drain above ground. The new drain piping would connect to the existing 4-inch main waste stack, eliminating the need for the drain line to run underground. Technician also recommends installing an air admittance valve (AAV) beneath the kitchen sink to provide proper venting for the drainage system. This will help maintain proper air flow within the drain piping and improve drainage performance for both the kitchen sink and laundry tub.

Technician found that the basement laundry tub/kitchen drain was backing up and draining slowly. Technician removed the existing P-trap from the laundry tub drain and used a cable machine to clear the drain line, which runs underground and connects to the existing cast-iron piping. While cabling the drain, technician encountered an obstruction approximately 10–15 feet into the underground drain line but was able to break through and clear the blockage. Technician continued running the cable through the drain line to the full length of the cable machine, approximately 70 feet, to help ensure the line was clear.

After completing the drain cleaning, technician reinstalled the P-trap and filled the laundry tub with water twice to test the drainage. Both tests confirmed that the water drained properly without backing up, indicating that the drain was flowing freely at the time of service.

LPH will rewire the unfinished basement and install six new dedicated circuits from the existing basement subpanel. This upgrade will provide properly distributed electrical service for the basement’s current and planned uses, reduce the electrical load on the existing circuits, and provide the appropriate protection for the new receptacles and connected equipment.

Basement Rewiring – Six New Circuits

1. Dedicated 15-Amp Radon Fan Circuit

* Install one new 15-amp circuit dedicated to the radon fan.
* Install a single receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall to provide a protected wiring method.

This dedicated circuit will provide a separate power source for the radon fan rather than relying on a shared circuit serving other basement equipment and receptacles.

2. Dedicated 20-Amp Exercise Area Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the basement exercise area.
* Install three receptacles to accommodate the designated exercise equipment.
* Install two receptacles along the wall bordering the mechanical room.
* Reuse the existing conduit at the designated location, remove the existing receptacle wiring, and install new wiring and a new receptacle.

Providing a dedicated circuit for the exercise area will help accommodate the electrical demand of the equipment without adding additional loads to the general basement receptacle circuit.

3. Dedicated 20-Amp Basement Kitchenette Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the planned basement kitchenette.
* Install two receptacle locations at the designated areas.
* Pick up the upstairs kitchen island receptacle as part of this circuit using wiring accessible from the basement.

Including the upstairs kitchen island receptacle on this new circuit will help remove its load from the existing circuit serving the basement lighting, screened-in porch, and existing exterior receptacles. This will help distribute the electrical demand more appropriately and reduce the likelihood of nuisance tripping on the existing circuit.

This circuit will provide a separate power source for the kitchenette and kitchen island receptacles, helping distribute the electrical load as the basement living space is developed.

4. Dedicated 20-Amp Fireplace Heater Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit dedicated to the basement fireplace heater.
* Install one receptacle at the designated location, with conduit piped down the wall.

A dedicated circuit will help accommodate the heater’s electrical demand without unnecessarily loading the general-purpose basement receptacle circuit.

5. Dedicated 20-Amp Exterior Hot Tub Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit from the basement subpanel, routed across the basement and drilled through the exterior wall to the back porch.
* Install one weather-resistant GFCI receptacle with an appropriate in-use bubble cover to supply the 120-volt inflatable hot tub.

Because this receptacle will serve equipment used around water, proper ground-fault protection is particularly important. GFCI protection is designed to quickly interrupt power when an electrical fault creates a potentially dangerous shock hazard.

The final circuit and receptacle arrangement will need to meet the hot tub manufacturer’s electrical requirements and applicable code requirements for the installation location.

6. Dedicated 20-Amp General Basement Receptacle Circuit

* Install one new 20-amp circuit to supply the remaining designated basement receptacles.
* Reuse the existing conduit at one location and install a new receptacle.
* Cut in one receptacle along the stairway wall.
* Install three additional receptacles at the designated locations, using conduit down the block walls as needed.

This additional circuit will provide convenient receptacle access throughout the basement while distributing the electrical demand across multiple circuits instead of continuing to rely on the existing overloaded arrangement.

Basement Circuit Protection

The six new circuits will be installed from the existing basement subpanel using the appropriate wiring methods and circuit protection for their intended applications. The estimate includes:

* Four 20-amp dual-function AFCI/GFCI circuit breakers.
* One 20-amp AFCI circuit breaker.
* One 15-amp AFCI circuit breaker.

AFCI protection is designed to detect certain dangerous electrical arcing conditions that can lead to fires. GFCI protection helps reduce the risk of electrical shock by detecting ground faults and interrupting power. Dual-function breakers combine both protective features in one device.

The specified breakers will provide the intended protection for the new circuits while helping bring the installation into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements.

Existing Basement Wiring – Junction Box Transition

Currently, one existing circuit supplies the basement lighting and receptacles, exterior receptacles, screened-in porch receptacles, and kitchen island receptacle. This places a substantial number of electrical loads on a single circuit and can contribute to nuisance tripping when multiple devices are operating.

As part of this project, LPH will disconnect and transition the existing basement wiring as necessary, installing accessible junction boxes along the basement ceiling to maintain continuity for the existing circuits. This will allow the existing wiring to remain operational while the new circuits take over the designated basement receptacle loads and the upstairs kitchen island receptacle is transferred to the new kitchenette circuit.

The goal is to distribute the electrical demand more appropriately, reduce the burden on the existing circuit, and provide a more functional electrical layout for the basement and the home’s connected areas.

Whole-Home Surge Protection Recommendation

With the installation of multiple new circuits and sensitive AFCI/GFCI protective devices, LPH recommends adding a whole-home surge protector at the main electrical panel.

Modern electrical equipment, appliances, and electronic circuit boards can be damaged by voltage surges originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, or electrical equipment cycling on and off within the home. These events can also contribute to premature wear or damage to sensitive electronic components.

A whole-home surge protector provides an additional layer of defense by helping divert damaging transient voltage away from the home’s electrical system and connected equipment. It is particularly beneficial for homes with modern appliances, HVAC equipment, electronics, and other sensitive devices.

Although surge protection cannot prevent every type of electrical disturbance or guarantee that equipment will never be damaged, it is a worthwhile protective upgrade for the home.

Additional 20-Amp Exterior Circuit From the Main Panel

LPH will install one additional 20-amp circuit from the main electrical panel to supply two receptacles serving the main garage area: one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel and one exterior receptacle on the opposite side of the wall.

This installation will include:

* Routing the new circuit from the main panel and dropping down the wall to the designated locations.
* Installing a GFCI-protected receptacle at the designated exterior location.
* Installing one receptacle inside the garage below the electrical panel.
* Providing convenient power sources for both interior garage and exterior use.
* Providing a more suitable power source for the garage microwave, reducing reliance on the existing garage door opener receptacle and extension cord.

Currently, the microwave is being powered through the garage door opener receptacle using an extension cord. This is not an ideal arrangement for an appliance that draws substantial current, particularly when the circuit may already be supplying other equipment. A properly installed receptacle on a new circuit will provide a more appropriate power source and help reduce nuisance tripping caused by shared electrical loads.

Exterior Receptacle Repairs and Weather Protection

LPH will also address the damaged exterior receptacles by replacing the existing devices with new weather-resistant receptacles and providing the required GFCI protection.

This portion of the work includes:

* Two weather-resistant GFCI receptacles.
* Two weather-resistant duplex receptacles.
* Reuse of the existing boxes and appropriate bubble covers where suitable.

Weather-resistant receptacles are designed to better withstand outdoor environmental exposure. Combined with appropriate GFCI protection and suitable covers, these replacements will help reduce the risk of moisture-related deterioration, electrical faults, and shock hazards.

The existing boxes are already equipped with appropriate bubble covers, so the existing covers will be retained where they are in suitable condition and compatible with the new receptacles.

Additional Grounding and Bonding Improvements

LPH recommends completing the home’s grounding and bonding system by installing a grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and adding approximately 5 feet of grounding conductor to bond the home’s gas piping system as required by applicable electrical code.

* Water Line Grounding: Install an approved grounding clamp on the existing metal water line and connect it to the home’s grounding electrode system as appropriate. This will address the incomplete grounding arrangement and help establish the required electrical connection to the metal water piping where applicable.
* Gas Line Bonding: Install approximately 5 feet of additional grounding conductor to properly bond the home’s gas piping system to the electrical grounding system, as required by applicable code provisions.

Proper grounding and bonding help provide a safe, intentional path for fault current, allowing protective devices to operate as intended during an electrical fault. These connections also help reduce dangerous voltage differences between metal piping systems and other grounded electrical components.

Completing these improvements will help bring the home’s grounding and bonding system into compliance with applicable electrical code requirements and provide an additional layer of protection for the home’s occupants and electrical equipment.

Installation, Testing, and Completion

All new circuits will be routed from the designated electrical panels using appropriate wiring methods, conduit, junction boxes, and circuit protection for their intended applications. LPH will complete the installation in accordance with applicable electrical code requirements, verify the new connections, and test the installed devices and circuits for proper operation.

The overall goal of this project is to provide a safer, more organized, and more functional electrical system for the unfinished basement and surrounding areas. By adding dedicated circuits for the radon fan, exercise equipment, kitchenette, fireplace heater, and hot tub, transferring the upstairs kitchen island receptacle to the new kitchenette circuit, expanding general receptacle capacity, and addressing the exterior electrical concerns, LPH will help accommodate the home’s electrical needs while reducing dependence on the existing heavily loaded circuit.

LPH will replace the existing expired smoke detectors throughout the home with new smoke detectors equipped with 10-year sealed lithium battery power. This upgrade will provide the homeowner with reliable smoke detection while eliminating the need for routine battery replacements over the detectors’ service life. All new detectors will be properly installed and tested to verify operation, helping maintain dependable early-warning protection for the home and its occupants.

LPH recommends replacing the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel with a brand-new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while retaining the home’s existing 200-amp service capacity.

Although the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is rated for 200 amps, its age and original design make replacement a worthwhile investment in the home’s electrical safety, reliability, and ability to accommodate modern electrical demands. Electrical panels are responsible for distributing power throughout the home and providing overcurrent protection to individual circuits. As panels age, breakers and internal connection points can experience wear, deterioration, and reduced reliability. Breaker connections on the bus bar can also loosen over time, potentially causing overheating, arcing, or unreliable circuit operation.

Why Upgrade the Existing Panel?

1. Aging Electrical Equipment

At approximately 34 years old, the existing Crouse-Hinds panel has provided decades of service. However, its age warrants consideration of replacement before deterioration or component failures create a more urgent situation. Replacing the panel allows LPH to install new equipment rather than continuing to depend on aging internal components and connections.

2. Better Support for Today’s Electrical Demands

Modern homes typically place greater demands on their electrical systems than they did decades ago. Today’s households rely on larger appliances, home office equipment, entertainment systems, exercise equipment, electronic devices, and other electrical loads that may not have been anticipated when the original panel was installed.

The existing panel’s 200-amp rating does not automatically mean the home needs a larger service. However, replacing the older panel provides an opportunity to improve circuit organization, evaluate the home’s electrical distribution, and accommodate additional circuit protection and future electrical projects where capacity permits.

3. Upgrade to a New 42-Space Eaton CH Panel

LPH will replace the existing Crouse-Hinds panel with a new 42-space Eaton CH panel. This provides a modern panel assembly with additional circuit spaces to help organize the home’s electrical system and accommodate future circuit additions, subject to the available service and load capacity.

The new panel will also provide a suitable platform for compatible circuit breakers and modern protective devices as needed for the home’s electrical requirements.

4. Improved Long-Term Reliability and Serviceability

Replacing the existing panel allows LPH to evaluate the incoming service conductors, grounding and bonding connections, neutral and ground terminations, and branch-circuit connections as part of the installation. This includes inspecting the breaker connections at the bus bar for looseness, signs of overheating, or other conditions that may affect safe operation. This helps identify concerns that may otherwise remain hidden within aging equipment.

A new panel can also make future electrical maintenance and troubleshooting more straightforward by providing current, compatible equipment and a more organized circuit layout.

5. Opportunity to Incorporate Whole-Home Surge Protection

As part of the panel replacement, LPH recommends installing whole-home surge protection to help protect sensitive electronics and appliances from damaging voltage transients originating from utility disturbances, lightning-related events, and electrical equipment cycling within the home.

Modern appliances and electronic equipment contain circuit boards and sensitive components that can be vulnerable to voltage surges. Whole-home surge protection provides an additional layer of defense for the home’s electrical system and connected equipment.

Scope of Work

LPH will:

* Remove the existing 34-year-old Crouse-Hinds electrical panel.
* Install a new 42-space Eaton CH electrical panel while maintaining the existing 200-amp service rating, provided the existing service components and installation support that configuration.
* Transfer the existing branch circuits to the new panel using compatible circuit breakers and appropriate wiring methods.
* Inspect breaker connections at the bus bar and address any loose, damaged, or overheated connections identified during the installation.
* Inspect and address grounding, bonding, neutral, and equipment grounding connections as required for the installation.
* Verify circuit identification and organize the panel directory.
* Evaluate the existing service connections and associated components for any additional concerns identified during replacement.
* Test the completed installation to verify proper operation.
* Provide whole-home surge protection as a recommended additional upgrade, if included in the approved scope.

The Long-Term Benefit

Replacing the existing Crouse-Hinds panel is a proactive investment in the home’s electrical infrastructure. Rather than waiting for aging equipment to develop a problem, the homeowner can move forward with a modern panel that offers additional circuit spaces, improved serviceability, and a better foundation for future electrical upgrades.

The goal is not simply to replace a panel because it is old. It is to update an aging, critical electrical component so the home’s distribution system is better positioned to serve the family’s current needs and future electrical demands.

Thank you for trusting LPH with your plumbing needs. We strive to provide professional, high-quality service on every visit, and your feedback helps us continue improving.

We would greatly appreciate hearing about your experience with the technician who served you today. Your feedback regarding the quality of work performed, communication, professionalism, and overall service is extremely valuable to us.

The homeowner was informed that the new hot and cold water lines installed approximately four years ago were reportedly not insulated. Technician inspected the underside of the mobile home and confirmed that the hot and cold water lines are insulated. Technician also verified that the heat tape installed on the water main is operational and that the heat tape outlet is functioning properly.

During the inspection, Technician observed that sections of the underside of the mobile home were missing insulation beneath the subfloor, as well as plastic sheeting. These missing materials may contribute to heat loss and increase the risk of the plumbing lines freezing during cold weather. Technician provided the homeowner with several referrals to assist with insulating the underside of the subfloor and providing additional protection for the existing hot and cold water lines.

Technician explained that if the homeowner is unable to find someone to complete the insulation work, Derrick may be able to assist with insulating the underside of the mobile home. However, LPH does not typically perform insulation work on mobile homes beyond insulating and protecting the water lines.

The homeowner also reported an issue with the electric heater located beneath the kitchen cabinet, which is not operating properly. An electrician is scheduled to visit the home on Monday to evaluate the heater and address the issue.
